passage:
"Divyansh, remember when you fell in the fish pond at Nani's?" Binita didi asked, grinning.
"No."
Two days later: "Remember the pond? You were all wet!"
Divyansh thought. "Maybe."
On Sunday she asked again. This time Divyansh said, "I fell in, and a fish touched my leg. It was cold."
Mummy looked up from the ironing. "Nani doesn't have a pond."
Divyansh frowned. "But I remember the fish."
Mummy sat down beside him. "Binita, no more pond stories, okay? Divyansh, you're not in trouble."

qa.q: Where did Binita say Divyansh fell in?
qa.a: Binita said Divyansh fell in the fish pond at Nani's.

qa.q: Why does Divyansh say, "But I remember the fish"?
qa.a: Divyansh feels confused and a little worried, because after being asked again and again, the imagined pond became a picture in his mind that feels just like a real memory.

qa.q: What did Mummy choose to do once she heard the fish story?
qa.a: She gently said Nani has no pond, asked Binita to stop the pond stories and told Divyansh he wasn't in trouble.

qa.q: How might Binita feel when Mummy asks for no more pond stories?
qa.a: Binita may feel a bit guilty or surprised, since it started as a joke, and realise how much the questions changed Divyansh's memory.

grounding: It shows a preschooler who, after being asked repeatedly about an event that never happened, begins to describe it as a memory.

passage:
Nursery teacher's note, Thursday
Several children kept asking Bhavna, "Did you see the dog in the classroom yesterday?" There was no dog. On Monday Bhavna said, "No." On Tuesday, "I think so." Today she told me it was brown, barked and ate her crayon.
She is not fibbing. She has heard the question so often that the picture feels real to her.
I told the class there was no dog, and asked them to ask each other, "What did you do?" instead. I have also told Bhavna's father, so he understands if the dog story comes home.
Minakshi

qa.q: What did Bhavna say the dog ate?
qa.a: Bhavna said it ate her crayon.

qa.q: Why does the dog story feel real to Bhavna?
qa.a: Bhavna feels confident and sincere about the dog, because she was asked so many times that a picture formed in her mind, and at her age that feels like remembering.

qa.q: What change did Minakshi make to how the children ask each other questions?
qa.a: Minakshi asked them to say "What did you do?" instead of "Did you see...?", which does not put a made-up event into anyone's head.

qa.q: Why is it helpful that Bhavna's father was told?
qa.a: If the dog story comes home, he will understand it without scolding her or worrying that something happened at school.

grounding: It shows a preschooler who, asked again and again about a dog that never came, starts to describe it in detail.

passage:
At the village well, Ritu's big cousins liked one question. "Ritu, you remember riding the temple elephant at the fair, na?"
Ritu, five, had only watched the elephant from far away, holding Kalyani Mausi's hand.
They asked every evening. By the end of the week, Ritu was telling the neighbours, "I sat on the elephant. It was very high, and it smelled like hay."
Kalyani Mausi listened, then crouched down. "We watched it from the sweet shop, remember? You ate jalebi."
Ritu looked puzzled, then pointed. "Jalebi, yes!"
That night Kalyani Mausi told the cousins, "No more elephant questions."

qa.q: Where did Kalyani Mausi say they watched the elephant from?
qa.a: From the sweet shop, where Ritu ate jalebi.

qa.q: Why might Ritu truly believe the elephant ride happened?
qa.a: Hearing the question every evening made the ride feel familiar, and at five Ritu's imagination and memory blended into one picture.

qa.q: How did Kalyani Mausi handle Ritu's elephant story?
qa.a: She crouched down, gently reminded Ritu of the real moment at the sweet shop and told the cousins to stop the elephant questions.

qa.q: What might the cousins learn when Kalyani Mausi stops their question?
qa.a: They may realise that their teasing question changed what Ritu remembered, which is not as harmless as it seemed.

grounding: It shows a preschooler who is asked repeatedly about a ride that never happened and begins to describe it as real.

passage: In their flat in Kyoto, Noa's cousin Ren loved one joke. "Noa, remember when the monkey stole your hat at the zoo?" Noa, five, had never been to the zoo. "No!" she said. A week later: "Remember the monkey? It ran up the tree!" Noa thought. "Maybe." By the third visit, Noa told her father, Hiroshi, "A monkey took my yellow hat and ran up a tree, and I cried." Hiroshi put down his chopsticks. "Noa, we've never been to the zoo." Noa looked confused. "But I remember the tree." Hiroshi gently asked Ren to stop the joke. That weekend he took Noa to the real zoo, and she held her yellow hat tightly.

qa.q: Where had Noa never been?
qa.a: To the zoo.

qa.q: Why does Noa say "But I remember the tree"?
qa.a: Being asked again and again made her imagine the scene, and the imagined picture now feels like a real memory to her.

qa.q: What did Hiroshi do after realising what had happened, and why was it wise?
qa.a: He gently asked Ren to stop the joke so the story wouldn't keep growing, and he didn't scold Noa, since she wasn't lying.

qa.q: How might Ren feel when asked to stop the joke?
qa.a: Ren might feel surprised and a little guilty, not having realised a joke could become something Noa truly believed.

grounding: A preschool girl repeatedly asked about a zoo trip that never happened begins to describe it as a real memory.

passage: At the kindergarten, Hafsa, the new assistant, had wrongly heard that Nitin had a birthday party at the weekend. On Monday she asked, "Nitin, did you have a big cake at your party?" Nitin, four, shook his head. On Tuesday: "Was it a train cake, with candles?" "Maybe." By Thursday, at circle time, Nitin announced, "My train cake had blue smoke, and I blew out five candles!" At pickup his mother looked puzzled. "His birthday's in March. There was no party." Hafsa's face fell. From then on she asked children only, "What did you do at the weekend?"

qa.q: When is Nitin's birthday?
qa.a: His birthday's in March.

qa.q: How did Nitin seem to feel when describing the train cake, and why?
qa.a: Nitin seemed excited and proud announcing the blue smoke and five candles, because Hafsa's repeated questions had made the imagined party feel like a memory.

qa.q: What change did Hafsa make, and why does it help?
qa.a: She began asking only open questions like "What did you do at the weekend?", which don't put ideas into a young child's head.

qa.q: How might Nitin's mother feel hearing about the party that never happened?
qa.a: She was puzzled and perhaps a little worried at first, then likely relieved to understand where the story came from.

grounding: A preschooler repeatedly asked about a party that never happened starts describing it in vivid detail.
